questions.prompt: What is the primary role of a Coordinator in iOS architecture?

options.text: Managing navigation flow and screen transitions outside of view controllers
options.explanation: Coordinators decouple navigation flow and dependency wiring from individual view controllers.

options.text: Rendering pixel graphics onto GPU textures
options.explanation: Pixel rendering is handled by Metal and Core Animation.

options.text: Managing database migrations in SQLite
options.explanation: Database migrations belong to the persistence layer.

options.text: Parsing remote JSON payloads into Swift structs
options.explanation: JSON parsing is performed by Codable in networking layers.

questions.prompt: Why is it problematic when a view controller directly instantiates and pushes the next screen?

options.text: It slows down CPU calculation speeds across the entire device
options.explanation: Direct navigation does not affect CPU clock speed.

options.text: It couples screens tightly together and prevents reusing the first screen in different flows
options.explanation: Direct instantiation forces a view controller to know its destination, ruining modularity.

options.text: It prevents the operating system from sending push notifications
options.explanation: Push notifications are independent of internal view controller routing.

options.text: It deletes view model state from memory
options.explanation: Pushing does not automatically delete view model state.

questions.prompt: How does a view or view model communicate navigation intent to a Coordinator?

options.text: By calling UIApplication.shared.openURL directly
options.explanation: openURL is for system-level URL handling, not internal coordinator communication.

options.text: By writing the destination screen name to disk storage
options.explanation: Disk storage is for persistence, not intra-module navigation signaling.

options.text: Through delegate protocols or closure callbacks
options.explanation: Views notify their coordinator of user actions using delegates or closures without knowing the destination.

options.text: By subclassing the destination view controller
options.explanation: Subclassing couples screens instead of decoupling them.

questions.prompt: Which UIKit component does a Coordinator typically manage to control screen presentation?

options.text: UIActivityIndicatorView
options.explanation: UIActivityIndicatorView displays loading spinners.

options.text: UILabel
options.explanation: UILabel displays static or dynamic text.

options.text: UIBezierPath
options.explanation: UIBezierPath defines vector drawing paths.

options.text: UINavigationController
options.explanation: A coordinator holds a reference to a UINavigationController to push and pop screens.

questions.prompt: What does a parent coordinator maintain to control the lifecycle of subordinate flows?

options.text: An array of child coordinators to keep them in memory until finished
options.explanation: Parent coordinators retain child coordinators in a collection so they are not deallocated prematurely.

options.text: A list of global notification observer tokens
options.explanation: Coordinators do not rely on global notification tokens for lifecycle control.

options.text: A persistent database connection table
options.explanation: Navigation state is runtime in-memory state.

options.text: A set of raw C memory pointers
options.explanation: Swift uses ARC reference management rather than raw C pointers.

questions.prompt: In modern SwiftUI, which view container enables programmatic, path-based navigation?

options.text: NavigationView
options.explanation: NavigationView is the legacy iOS 13-15 container, deprecated in favor of NavigationStack.

options.text: NavigationStack
options.explanation: NavigationStack (iOS 16+) supports data-driven navigation bound to a collection of routes.

options.text: TabView
options.explanation: TabView manages separate tab items rather than a stack-based navigation path.

options.text: ScrollView
options.explanation: ScrollView provides scrolling behavior for content.

questions.prompt: What requirement must route enum cases satisfy to work with NavigationStack and navigationDestination?

options.text: They must inherit from NSObject
options.explanation: Swift enums cannot inherit from NSObject.

options.text: They must conform to CoreData.NSManagedObject
options.explanation: Routes are lightweight value types, not persistent managed objects.

options.text: They must conform to Hashable
options.explanation: NavigationStack requires items in the path and navigation destinations to be Hashable.

options.text: They must be declared as global mutable variables
options.explanation: Routes should be immutable values stored in a path collection.

questions.prompt: How does a SwiftUI Router implement a popToRoot action?

options.text: By closing the app process immediately
options.explanation: Closing the process crashes the app and violates Apple guidelines.

options.text: By reloading the main UIWindow scene
options.explanation: Reloading the scene is a heavy UIKit workaround rather than idiomatic SwiftUI navigation.

options.text: By presenting a full screen modal over the stack
options.explanation: Presenting a modal does not clear the underlying stack.

options.text: By emptying the bound navigation path array
options.explanation: Clearing the path array causes NavigationStack to pop back to the root view automatically.

questions.prompt: What is the advantage of using NavigationLink(value:) over NavigationLink(destination:)?

options.text: It resolves destination views lazily and decouples presentation from routing data
options.explanation: NavigationLink(value:) pairs with .navigationDestination to instantiate views on demand.

options.text: It bypasses the SwiftUI layout pass entirely
options.explanation: All views still participate in the SwiftUI layout system.

options.text: It converts SwiftUI views into Objective-C nib files
options.explanation: NavigationLink does not convert views into nibs.

options.text: It disables animation on all screen transitions
options.explanation: Transitions remain animated by default.

questions.prompt: What common memory leak occurs in UIKit Coordinator architectures?

options.text: Allocating too many integers on the call stack
options.explanation: Stack memory cleans up automatically on function return.

options.text: Failing to remove finished child coordinators from the parent coordinator's array
options.explanation: Retaining child coordinators after their screens pop leaks the coordinator and its view controllers.

options.text: Using struct value types for coordinators
options.explanation: Coordinators are classes to maintain reference identity.

options.text: Declaring coordinator delegates as weak
options.explanation: Weak delegates prevent retain cycles; strong delegates cause them.

questions.prompt: How can a Coordinator detect when a user taps the UIKit back button to clean up child coordinators?

options.text: By polling the navigation stack count in a background timer loop
options.explanation: Polling timers waste CPU and battery resources.

options.text: By overriding the deinit of UIApplication
options.explanation: UIApplication deinit cannot be overridden.

options.text: By acting as the UINavigationControllerDelegate and inspecting popped view controllers
options.explanation: Intercepting navigationController(_:didShow:animated:) reveals which view controller was dismissed.

options.text: By disabling the interactive back swipe gesture
options.explanation: Disabling the gesture damages user experience and does not fix cleanup.

questions.prompt: What happens if a child coordinator holds a strong reference back to its parent coordinator?

options.text: The app crashes on startup with an unrecognized selector error
options.explanation: Reference cycles do not cause unrecognized selector crashes.

options.text: The compiler refuses to build the module
options.explanation: Swift permits strong reference cycles at compile time.

options.text: Swift automatically converts one reference into a weak reference
options.explanation: Swift ARC requires developers to declare weak references explicitly.

options.text: A retain cycle occurs, preventing both coordinators from deallocating
options.explanation: Mutual strong references create a retain cycle that leaks both objects.

questions.lessonSection: How to answer in the interview
questions.prompt: How do navigation patterns simplify implementing deep links in iOS apps?

options.text: A central coordinator or router can parse a URL and programmatically construct a complete stack of screens
options.explanation: Decoupled navigation allows building multi-level navigation stacks from URL routes without loading intermediate screens manually.

options.text: Deep links only work when using storyboard segues
options.explanation: Storyboard segues make programmatic deep link assembly harder, not easier.

options.text: Coordinators automatically register URL schemes in the Info.plist
options.explanation: Info.plist configuration is a build-time bundle setting, not handled by coordinators.

options.text: Deep links bypass all authentication checks when using coordinators
options.explanation: Coordinators help enforce authentication guards on deep links.

questions.lessonSection: How to answer in the interview
questions.prompt: Why is the Coordinator pattern valuable when migrating an app gradually from UIKit to SwiftUI?

options.text: Because it forces all SwiftUI views to compile as UIViews
options.explanation: SwiftUI views remain declarative structs.

options.text: Because coordinators can wrap SwiftUI views in UIHostingController and push them alongside UIKit screens
options.explanation: Coordinators manage the shared navigation controller, seamlessly mixing UIKit controllers and hosted SwiftUI views.

options.text: Because coordinators delete the UIKit runtime automatically
options.explanation: UIKit remains active and loaded.

options.text: Because SwiftUI cannot be used without a UIKit coordinator
options.explanation: SwiftUI has native navigation tools like NavigationStack.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between UIKit Coordinators and SwiftUI NavigationRouters?

options.text: UIKit Coordinators are written in C, while SwiftUI Routers are written in Swift
options.explanation: Both are implemented in Swift.

options.text: SwiftUI Routers cannot handle modal sheets
options.explanation: SwiftUI Routers can manage sheet presentation states.

options.text: Coordinators push imperative view controllers, while SwiftUI Routers manipulate declarative path state
options.explanation: Coordinators call imperative UIKit methods, whereas SwiftUI routers update data arrays bound to declarative stacks.

options.text: Coordinators cannot support back buttons
options.explanation: Coordinators work alongside standard navigation back buttons.
